extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers interested in standards for good poetry / literary instruction (Renaissance literary theory)
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating poetry's moral and formal qualities
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging and composing poetry focused on moral instruction, persuasive power (moving to action), formal workmanship (verse, proportion), and genre-appropriate effects. Derived from an essay-length defense of poetry comparing poets to philosophers and historians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feigning notable images of virtues and vices with delightful teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should 'feign notable images of virtues, vices, or what else, with that delightful teaching' — i.e., present moral qualities through imaginative representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet's work is to create invented images or fictions that display virtues and vices in a way that both delights and instructs; the combination of pleasure and moral example is central to the poet’s authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner: piece each syllable by just proportion according to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry's manner must not be 'table-talk fashion' or loose speech, but 'piecing each syllable of each word by just proportion, according to the dignity of the subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal workmanship matters: verse, rhythm, diction and proportion should be fitted to the subject’s dignity; careful metrical and linguistic control distinguishes poetical speech from casual talk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's educative ends: purifying wit, enriching memory, enabling judgment, enlarging conceit
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of learning which poetry serves is 'this purifying of wit, this enriching of memory, enabling of judgment, and enlarging of conceit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess poetry by its capacity to improve intellectual and moral faculties — it should sharpen wit, fix things in memory, enable sound judgment, and enlarge the imaginative reach (conceit) of the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine precept and example (poet as moderator between philosopher and historian)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'doth the peerless' task of uniting the philosopher’s precept with the historian’s example by giving a perfect picture which couples general notions with particular exemplars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong poem supplies the abstract teaching of philosophy in concrete, pictured exemplars — it should both explain what ought to be (precept) and show how it appears in action (example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid imagery to make abstract notions perceptible
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'yieldeth to the powers of the mind an image' of a thing where a philosopher's definitions would remain 'dark before the imaginative and judging power.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well a poem makes abstract moral or intellectual ideas intelligible via sensory, pictorial, or dramatic images (e.g., Ajax’s madness, Œdipus’s remorse). Vivid representation that 'strikes, pierces, and possesses the sight of the soul' is prized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and popular persuasion (poet as popular philosopher)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is 'the food for the tenderest stomachs; the right popular philosopher' — able to instruct those who cannot grasp philosophical abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poetry for its ability to reach broad and non-scholarly audiences (fables, parables, tales) — clarity and engaging form that bring moral lessons to ordinary readers are virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim at universals rather than mere particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Aristotle’s idea that poetry is 'more philosophical' because it deals with the universal (καθολου), whereas history treats the particular (καθ ἕκαστον).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should communicate general truths and patterns of human behavior rather than only recording singular events; prefer works that illustrate what ought to be or what is generally true over mere chronicle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame feigned examples to the most reasonable / idealized case
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may shape feigned (fictional) examples to represent what should be done — often better for teaching than strict historic truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether fictional examples are constructed to exemplify ideal or instructive conduct (e.g., feigned Cyrus or Æneas) so readers learn the right rule by a clear, representative instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to move readers to practice (praxis over knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest aim is not mere knowledge (γνῶσις) but action (πρᾶξις); the poet 'moveth' as much as he 'teacheth,' and moving is prerequisite to being taught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the poem motivates readers toward virtuous action, not just intellectual assent; persuasive emotional and imaginative force is a key metric of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with delight (music, tale) rather than obscure definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'doth not begin with obscure definitions' but with 'words set in delightful proportion... and with a tale' to win the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value narrative, musicality, and pleasurable form as means to entice and retain learners; a poem that teaches by delight is superior to one that begins with abstruse theoretical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make even horrible matters instructive by poetic imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetical imitation can render 'those things which in themselves are horrible... made... delightful' so they instruct without repelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how the poem transforms repellent or difficult material into a form through which readers can apprehend moral lessons — skillful aesthetic rendering is praiseworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral clarity: mark what to be followed and what to be shunned
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should lay virtues, vices, and passions 'so in their own natural states laid to the view, that we seem not to hear of them, but clearly to see through them' — showing what to emulate and avoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge clarity of moral delineation: characters and actions should be presented so their moral status (worthy or blameworthy) is evident and instructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate poet by his works first, then by his parts
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It shall not be amiss, first, to weight this latter sort of poetry by his works, and then by his parts;' assess the whole before dissecting components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should consider overall effectiveness (does the completed work teach and delight?) before parsing formal elements; conversely, if the whole fails, inspect parts for defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing genres acceptable if each element is well-executed
rubrics_metrics.description: Some poesies 'have coupled together two or three kinds' (tragical and comical, prose and verse) and 'if severed they be good, the conjunction cannot be hurtful.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hybrid works are permissible provided each constituent mode/part is accomplished; judge whether the fusion preserves the strengths of each genre rather than degrading them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral should use humble speech to expose social misery and moral lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: The pastoral, through humble voices (Melibæus, Tityrus), can 'show the misery of people under hard lords and ravening soldiers' and illustrate patience, contentment, and injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess pastoral poems by their capacity to make political and moral truths intelligible via rustic disguise: the simpler form should illuminate larger social concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegiac (lament) should move pity and rightly accompany causes of lamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The elegiac 'in a kind heart, would move rather pity than blame' and is praised for compassionately accompanying just causes of lament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge elegies by sincerity and the aptness of mourning: they should evoke appropriate sorrow and reflection without excess or trivialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iambic verse should rebuke vice and 'rub the galled mind'
rubrics_metrics.description: The iambic 'rubs the galled mind, making shame the trumpet of villany' by boldly exposing and censuring wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate iambic or invective poetry for its effectiveness in chastising vice — clarity, sting, and corrective force are desirable, while empty insult is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should touch vice playfully to make men laugh at folly
rubrics_metrics.description: The satiric 'Omne vafer vitium ridenti tangit amico' — it sportingly touches vices so the reader laughs at folly and becomes ashamed of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good satire balances humor and reproach: it should reveal folly sympathetically enough that readers self-recognize and reform, rather than merely insulting targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy should imitate common errors to correct them and provide foils for virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is 'an imitation of the common errors of our life' that represents domestic faults (niggardly Demea, crafty Davus) so the beholder cannot be content to be such a one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge comedies by how effectively they expose everyday vices and foibles, providing recognizable signs of folly that encourage audiences to avoid them; the comic should instruct via ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy should open wounds, evoke pity and fear, and teach the uncertainty of worldly fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy 'openeth the greatest wounds... that with stirring the effects of admiration and commiseration, teacheth the uncertainty of this world' and can move even hardened men to pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tragedy by its power to move (catharsis), its moral teaching about human limitation and fortune, and the seriousness and dignity of its representation; emotional effect that leads to reflection is key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyric (song) should praise virtue, raise thoughts, and awaken courage
rubrics_metrics.description: The lyric 'giveth praise, the reward of virtue... sometimes raiseth up his voice to the height of the heavens' and can 'awake the thoughts from the sleep of idleness' (e.g., Pindaric songs of ancestors' valour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lyrics by their emotive elevation and ability to inspire public or private virtues through song; appropriateness of tone and evocative musical language matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroical poetry as supreme: models magnanimity and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroical 'teacheth and moveth to the most high and excellent truth: who maketh magnanimity and justice shine' (exemplified by Achilles, Æneas, Cyrus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge epic/heroical works by their capacity to present noble exemplars whose actions instruct readers in the highest virtues and provide comprehensive models of conduct across situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction itself is not corrupting if description and end contain no evil
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 'neither his description nor end containeth any evil, the thing described cannot be evil' — mere depiction of vile acts is not blameworthy if the poem’s purpose and portrayal are morally directed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider authorial intention and moral framing: representations of vice are permissible when they clearly serve instructive ends (to condemn or warn), not to celebrate wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical mastery and accomplishment distinguish good poets from many who fail
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of poetry may be excellent, but 'by few men that art can be accomplished' — faults often lie in execution, not in the art’s principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both the inherent merits of poetic principles and the poet’s skillful realization; criticize technical failings (tone, form, coherence) as distinct from the theory of poetry itself.
